import numpy as np
from PyLTSpice import RawRead
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

raw = RawRead("./ngspice/NMOS.raw", dialect="ngspice")

par_names = raw.get_trace_names()

par_prefix = par_names[1].split('[')[0]

short_names = {}
for name in par_names:
    short_name = name.split('[', 1)[1].split(']', 1)[0] if '[' in name and ']' in name else name
    short_names[short_name] = name


var1 = raw.get_trace(short_names["id"]).get_wave()
var2 = raw.get_trace(short_names["vds"]).get_wave()
var3 = raw.get_trace(short_names["vgs"]).get_wave()
sweep = raw.get_trace(short_names["v(v-sweep)"]).get_wave()

v_sweep = np.array(list(dict.fromkeys(sweep)))

var1 = np.reshape(var1, (len(v_sweep), -1), order='F')
var2 = np.reshape(var2, (len(v_sweep), -1), order='F')
var3 = np.reshape(var3, (len(v_sweep), -1), order='F')
vgs = var3[0, :]


plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
plt.plot(var2, var1 * 1000)
plt.legend([f"VGS = {v:.2f} V" for v in vgs])

plt.xlabel("Vds (V)")
plt.ylabel("Id (mA)")
plt.grid(True)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Drain current \(I_D\) versus drain-source voltage \(V_{DS}\) for different \(V_{GS}\) values.






#target curve
target_vgs = 0.8
idx = np.argmin(np.abs(vgs - target_vgs))

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
plt.plot(var2[:, idx], var1[:, idx] * 1000)
plt.legend([f"VGS = {vgs[idx]:.2f} V"])

plt.xlabel("Vds (V)")
plt.ylabel("Id (mA)")
plt.grid(True)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 2: Drain current \(I_D\) versus drain-source voltage \(V_{DS}\) for \(V_{GS}=0.8\).

from scipy.interpolate import PchipInterpolator

var1 = raw.get_trace(short_names["gm"]).get_wave()
var2 = raw.get_trace(short_names["vgs"]).get_wave()
var3 = raw.get_trace(short_names["vds"]).get_wave()
var4 = raw.get_trace(short_names["gds"]).get_wave()
sweep = raw.get_trace(short_names["v(v-sweep)"]).get_wave()

v_sweep = np.array(list(dict.fromkeys(sweep)))

var1 = np.reshape(var1, (len(v_sweep), -1), order='F')

var3 = np.reshape(var3, (len(v_sweep), -1), order='F')
var4 = np.reshape(var4, (len(v_sweep), -1), order='F')

vds = var3.T[0, :]

#target curve
target_vds = 1.8
idx = np.argmin(np.abs(vds - target_vds))

x = var2.T[:, idx]
y = var1.T[:, idx]/var4.T[:, idx]

x_smooth = np.linspace(x.min(), x.max(), 100)
interp = PchipInterpolator(x, y)
y_smooth = interp(x_smooth)

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
plt.plot(x_smooth, y_smooth)
plt.legend([f"VDS = {vds[idx]:.2f} V"])

plt.xlabel("Vgs (V)")
plt.ylabel("gm/gds")
plt.grid(True)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Introduction to Analog Circuit Design
text:
Getting started
To start designing analog circuits, you need to understand the fundamentals of electronic circuits, including nodal and mesh analysis, Kirchhoff’s Current Law (KCL) and Kirchhoff’s Voltage Law (KVL), and, of course, transistors and other nonlinear devices.
Furthermore, you should be able to design and analyze basic circuit blocks using pen and paper. In other words, you should be able to understand and predict the behavior and functionality of basic circuit blocks before simulating them.
After designing a circuit, its functionality is verified through simulation, and modifications are made as necessary to achieve the desired performance. Therefore, we need a circuit simulator. Two popular simulators for analog IC design are Synopsys HSPICE and Cadence Spectre. Unfortunately, both of these tools require a paid license.
Fortunately, there are several free circuit simulators available for analog circuit design. Ngspice and LTspice are two well-known free SPICE circuit simulators. With LTspice, schematic capture and waveform viewing are integrated into the simulator. Ngspice, on the other hand, is primarily a SPICE-based simulator whose input is a circuit netlist and whose output consists of simulation data. Therefore, to work with schematics, you need a schematic capture tool, and to view simulation waveforms, you need a waveform viewer. In this course, we use Ngspice as the circuit simulator.
For schematic capture, there is a free and open-source tool called Xschem. Since Xschem supports hierarchical schematics, it is well suited for designing large and complex circuits. It is also supported by several open-source PDKs. Furthermore, Xschem provides an integrated waveform viewer, while also supporting external waveform viewers.
It is recommended to install Linux, as all of the essential tools run smoothly on Linux-based systems. Linux distributions are free, and if you are using Windows, you can easily set up a Linux environment through WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux). For example, I am using Ubuntu on WSL.
Below are the main tools used in a typical analog IC design flow:

Schematic Capture:
xschem — https://xschem.sourceforge.io/stefan/index.html
Circuit Simulation:
ngspice — https://ngspice.sourceforge.io
Layout Editor:
Magic VLSI — http://opencircuitdesign.com/magic/index.html
Open PDK:
SkyWater SKY130 — http://opencircuitdesign.com/open_pdks/index.html



Integrating Xschem with SKY130
There are clear instructions available for setting up xschem with the SKY130 PDK:
Documentation:
XSCHEM SKY130 INTEGRATION
A detailed video tutorial is also available, covering xschem, ngspice, and SKY130 PDK usage from scratch:
https://youtu.be/bYbkz8FXnsQ?si=K5OG5g5v23BnFscz

Welcome to ACC Designs R&D!
This is my personal website dedicated to my work and activities in Analog Custom Circuit Design. It primarily covers Analog and Mixed-Signal IC Design, including topics such as data converters, RF circuits and blocks, various types of amplifiers, and more.
The website also covers selected topics in discrete circuit design, including basic analog circuit design, power electronics, and switching-mode power supplies (SMPS).

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
We will extract the small-signal characteristics of MOSFETs using freely available, open-source PDKs and CAD tools. The analysis is carried out using the SkyWater sky130 PDK, Xschem as the schematic capture tool, and Ngspice as the circuit simulator.
All tools (Xschem, Ngspice, and sky130 PDK) must be installed properly on a Linux system. In this overview, Ubuntu running under WSL is used. The installation procedure is discussed in a separate article.
The reader is assumed to have a basic understanding of MOSFET device physics and the fundamentals of MOSFET operation. Figure 1 illustrates the structure and symbols of NMOS and PMOS devices. In integrated-circuit design, a MOSFET has four terminals: gate (G), source (S), drain (D), and bulk (B). Modern CMOS technologies typically employ a p-type substrate; therefore, the bulk of all NMOS devices (except native devices) is tied to the substrate, i.e., GND or VSS. In contrast, PMOS devices are fabricated in isolated wells, allowing their bulks to be biased independently.

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Saturation region:
Including channel length modulation, the mosfet current is given by:
\[
I_D=\frac{1}{2}\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}\left(V_{GS}-V_{TH}\right)^2(1+\lambda\ V_{DS})
\tag{3}\]
The parameter \(\lambda\) is the channel-length modulation coefficient, which decreases with increasing channel length.
\[
\lambda\propto\frac{1}{L}
\tag{4}\]

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Body effect:
Increasing the source-to-bulk voltage raises the threshold voltage:
\[
V_{TH}=V_{TH0}+\gamma\left(\sqrt{2\Phi_F+V_{SB}}-\sqrt{\left|2\Phi_F\right|}\right)
\tag{5}\]
\[
\gamma=\frac{\sqrt{2q\epsilon_{si}N_{sub}}}{C_{ox}}\approx0.3\ to\ 0.4\ \left(V^\frac{1}{2}\right)
\tag{6}\]
\[
V_{TH0}=\Phi_{MS}+2\Phi_F+\frac{Q_{dep}}{C_{ox}}=V_{TH}\ when\ V_{SB}=0
\tag{7}\]

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Subthreshold (weak inversion):
When \(V_{GS} \approx V_{TH}\), the device enters weak inversion, and the drain current follows:
\[
I_D=I_0\exp{\frac{V_{GS}}{\xi V_T}}
\tag{8}\]
where \(I_0\) is proportional to \(W/L\), \(\xi > 1\), and \(V_T=kT/q\). The device is said to operate in weak inversion, as opposed to strong inversion.

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Equations:
In triode region, a MOSFET behaves as a voltage-controlled resistor:
\[
R_{on}=\frac{1}{\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS}-V_{TH})}
\tag{9}\]
In saturation, the transconductance is:
\[
g_m=\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{GS}}
\tag{10}\]
Equivalent expressions include:
\[
g_m=\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{GS}-V_{TH})
\tag{11}\]
\[
g_m=\sqrt{2\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}I_D}
\tag{12}\]
\[
g_m=\frac{2I_D}{V_{GS}-V_{TH}}
\tag{13}\]
The output resistance due to channel-length modulation is:
\[
r_o=\frac{1}{g_{ds}}=\frac{\partial V_{DS}}{\partial I_D}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{2}\mu_nC_{ox}\frac{W}{L}\left(V_{GS}-V_{TH}\right)^2\times\lambda}
\tag{14}\]
Given \(\lambda V_{DS} << 1\), we have
\[
r_o=\frac{1}{g_{ds}}=\frac{1+\lambda V_{DS}}{\lambda I_D}\approx\frac{1}{\lambda I_D}
\tag{15}\]
The body-effect transconductance is:
\[
g_{mb}=\frac{\partial I_D}{\partial V_{BS}}=gm\frac{\gamma}{2\sqrt{2\Phi_F+V_{SB}}}=\eta\ g_m
\tag{16}\]

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Long-channel NMOS:
The circuit in Figure 3 is used to evaluate the small-signal, low frequency behavior of an NMOS device. Because capacitances are not considered in this section, DC-sweep analysis is employed.






Figure 3: Simple NMOS circuit used for DC-sweep analysis



Here, W/L = 100u/1.5u, number of gates (fingers) are 10, and the VGS sweep ranges from 0 to 1.8V. Figure 4 shows gm and gds of the NMOS versus VGS.












(a) \(g_m\) versus \(V_{GS}\)











(b) \(g_{ds}\) versus \(V_{GS}\)






Figure 4: Variation of \(g_m\) and \(g_{ds}\) versus \(V_{GS}\) for \(V_{DS}=1V\).





In this circuit, \(V_{TH} \approx 470mV\). As \(V_{GS}\) increases, both \(g_m\) and \(g_{ds}\) increase as expected. It’s interesting to see the gds – Id relationship as shown in Figure 5. The curve is nearly linear, and according to Equation 15, its slope corresponds to the channel-length modulation coefficient \(\lambda\).









Figure 5: Variation of \(g_{ds}\) versus Drain current \(I_d\) for \(V_{DS}=1.8V\).






The intrinsic small-signal gain of a MOSFET is defined as
\[
A_v = g_mr_o = \frac{g_m}{g_{ds}}
\tag{17}\]
The intrinsic gain of a long-channel NMOS transistor is shown in Figure 6. As can be seen, in saturation region, the gain peaks at approximately \(V_{GS}=0.56V\). This corresponds to an overdrive voltage of \(V_{ov}=V_{GS}-V_{TH}\approx 100mV\), at which the device achieves its maximum intrinsic gain. As \(V_{ov}\) increases further, the intrinsic gain decreases.









Figure 6: Intrinsic small-signal low-frequency gain of NMOS with W/L = 100u/1.5u.






For \(V_{ov}\) below roughly 80mV the device operates in the weak-inversion region. When \(V_{GS}<V_{TH}\), the transistor is off and the concept of intrinsic gain is no longer meaningful.

title: MOSFET Small-Signal Characteristics
text:
Short-channel NMOS:
For channel length below \(1\mu m\) (submicron), MOSFET behavior is significantly affected by short-channel and other higher-order effects. Figure 7 illustrates how these effects alter the small-signal parameters of a device with \(W/L = 10\mu m/ 0.15\mu m\). A detailed discussion of short-channel devices will be presented in a subsequent article.
